title: Where the Moths Sleep
creature: Moths that carry dreams people dropped
summary: Ines finds the attic full of pale moths, and every one of them is holding a dream that somebody forgot.

chapters.title: The Attic Light
chapters.text: The attic light had been left on for as long as anyone could remember, and nobody could say who had done it. It bothered Ines more than it bothered anybody else. She had asked her uncle about it twice. The first time he had said it was cheaper than arguing about it, which was not an answer. The second time he had said that some things in a house are older than the people in it, which was less of an answer than the first one but sounded more like one. She could see it at night from the garden — a thin orange line around the edge of the trapdoor, hanging in the dark of the landing ceiling like a picture of a door rather than a door. She went up on the first warm night of the year, because the trapdoor had begun to hum. That was new. It was a low sound, not electrical, more like the noise a bee makes inside a jam jar three rooms away. It had started on the Tuesday and by the Friday she could feel it in the ladder rungs. She waited until her uncle had gone out to lock the greenhouse, and then she went up. The attic was full of moths. Not fluttering. Not knocking themselves stupid against the bulb, which is what moths do and the only thing Ines had ever seen them do. These were resting. Hundreds of them, folded flat against the rafters and the underside of the roof slates, wings closed, absolutely still, arranged the way pages are arranged in a book. They were the colour of old paper — some almost white, some the yellow of a page that has been in a window, a few nearly brown. They did not startle when her head came up through the hatch. One near her hand adjusted itself very slightly, the way a person shifts in a chair. She sat on the edge of the hatch with her legs down through it, because the floor did not look trustworthy, and she looked at the one nearest to her. There was something on its wings. Not a pattern. She knew what moth patterns looked like: eyes and speckles and the little false faces. This was a picture. A very small one, painted in the way a stamp is printed, right across both wings so that the join ran through the middle of it. It was a kitchen. A yellow kitchen with a window over the sink and a chair pulled out from the table. She looked at the next one. A boat, on a grey sea, seen from behind. She looked at the next one, and it was a face she almost knew, and then did not, and the almost stayed with her all the way down the ladder.

chapters.title: A Dream Someone Dropped
chapters.text: She went up again the next night, and the night after that. By the fourth night she had worked out how to pick one up. You do not catch a moth; you put your finger against the wall beside it and wait, and eventually it walks onto you, unhurried, like somebody stepping onto a bus. The one that came onto her finger on the fourth night had a hallway painted across its wings. A long hallway with a runner carpet, and at the end of it, a green door. She held it under the bulb and looked at it for a long time. The longer she looked, the more certain she became that she had walked down that hallway. She knew what the light was like at the far end in the afternoon. She knew the carpet had a worn patch two thirds of the way along and that you could feel it through socks. And at exactly the same time, with exactly the same certainty, she knew that she had never been there in her life. Her uncle came up the ladder behind her with two mugs of tea, which is a difficult thing to do and suggested practice. He did not seem surprised by any of it. He handed her a mug, sat down on an upturned crate that had clearly been sat on many times before, and looked at the moth on her finger. "Green door," he said. "That's a good one. Somebody misses that." Ines said nothing, because she could not think of a question small enough to start with. "People drop dreams," her uncle said. "All the time. The way you drop a glove out of a pocket — you don't feel it go, you just find later that you've only got the one. Wake up too fast, somebody says your name, the alarm goes off in the wrong part of it. And the dream falls out." He drank some tea. "They have to go somewhere. Everything has to go somewhere. This house has been collecting them since before it was mine, and before it was my mother's, and I've never worked out why this house and not the one next door." "How many are there?" "I stopped counting in about nineteen ninety." Ines turned her hand slowly so the moth stayed level. On the wall above her, a hundred pale wings held a hundred small pictures: a bicycle, a hospital corridor, a hillside with a wall across it, a wedding, a dog, a shop she was almost sure was the shop on Bridge Street but with different windows. "Can they go back?" she said. "Can you give one back to someone?" Her uncle looked at his tea for a while. "That," he said, "is the difficult part."

chapters.title: The Face She Almost Knew
chapters.text: The one she wanted was the face. She had found it on the first night — third along the rafter, near the chimney breast — and she had gone back to it every night since, and every night the same thing happened. She would look at it and think *oh, that's* — and then the name would not arrive. It was a man. Middle-aged, or getting there. Dark hair going back at the front. He was looking slightly to the left of whoever was dreaming him, and he was in the middle of saying something, and his eyebrows were up. It was painted better than the others. That was the strange part. The kitchen and the boat and the green door were all painted the way a thing is painted from memory — the important bits sharp, everything else vague. This one had a collar on his shirt with a button missing at the point, and a small scar through one eyebrow, and the sort of detail you only get when somebody has looked at a face for years and years and years. She asked her uncle who it was. He came up and looked at it for a while with his hands in his pockets and said he had no idea, and that he had been wondering about that one himself since about 2003. She did the sensible thing, which took her three weeks. She drew it — badly, then less badly, then on the fourth attempt well enough to be recognisable — and she carried the drawing round the town in her coat pocket and showed it to people. The woman at the bakery said no. The man at the bicycle shop said no, and then held the drawing at arm's length and said no again, more slowly. The librarian said he looked like somebody's brother, which was not useful. Father Costa said he looked like everybody's brother, which was less useful still. A man at the bus stop said it was a very good drawing, which she appreciated but could not do anything with. At the end of three weeks she had shown it to thirty-one people and none of them knew him. She sat on the wall outside the chemist with the drawing on her knee and worked it out, and she did not enjoy working it out. There were only two ways it went. Either the person who had dropped that dream had moved away — in which case the moth would sit on that rafter until the house fell down. Or the person who had dropped it was dead, and the dream had come loose the way the last of anything comes loose, and it had come up the hill and in under the slates and folded itself against a beam, and there was nobody left in the world who could be given it. She went home and up the ladder and sat on the edge of the hatch for a long time. Her uncle came up eventually with the tea. He did not ask how it had gone; he had clearly worked out how it had gone from the fact that she was sitting in the dark. "There are about four hundred like that," he said. "That I know of. Ones nobody claims. They don't go anywhere. They don't die, as far as I can tell — I've got one up there with a horse and cart on it and there hasn't been a cart on this hill since before the war." "So what are they for?" "They're not *for* anything," he said. "That's the bit that took me longest. I spent about fifteen years trying to make this place useful and I got nowhere, because I was asking the wrong question." He nodded up at the rafters. "It's not a lost property office. Nobody's coming to the desk. It's just where they end up." Ines looked at the man with his eyebrows up, in the middle of saying something, to somebody who had loved him enough to keep the missing button. "That's sad," she said. "It is," her uncle agreed. "But look at the state of him. Somebody was extremely fond of that man. That's still true. It's true right now, on that rafter, whether or not anybody comes for it." He drank his tea. "There are worse things to have a house full of."

chapters.title: Giving It Back
chapters.text: It took most of the summer to work out, and the working out was not magical in the least. It was mostly asking people awkward questions and being wrong. The rules, as far as Ines ever established them, were these. A moth would not go to just anyone. You could carry one out in your cupped hands to a person and open your hands and it would sit there like a scrap of paper, entirely uninterested, and eventually walk back up your sleeve. It had to be dusk. Not dark, not evening — dusk, the twenty minutes when the streetlights are on but you can still see the colour of things. And you had to be standing near where the person had been when they lost it. That was the part that made it hard, because it meant working out who, which meant asking, and there is no good way to ask an adult whether they have recently mislaid a dream about a boat. She got round it by asking about the pictures instead. The woman at the bakery, when Ines described a grey sea seen from the back of a boat, stopped counting change and said, "My father had a boat like that," and then, "Why?" — and Ines said she had seen a painting, which was a lie, but only a small one. She let the boat moth go outside the bakery at dusk on a Thursday. It went in through the top window, which was open for the heat, and did not come out. The man who fixed bicycles had lost the hallway with the green door. She was almost sure before she asked him and completely sure afterwards, from the way he said "that was my grandmother's house" and then stopped talking and went back to truing the wheel he had been truing. She let it go outside his shop the following evening. He was still there, working late, and he did not see her do it. She watched from across the road as the moth went in under the shutter. He came out about a minute later and stood on the pavement, looking at nothing in particular, for quite a long time. Then he went back in and got on with the wheel. He never mentioned it to her, and she never mentioned it to him, and for about a year afterwards he did her brake cables for nothing and neither of them ever said why. She did nineteen that summer. Nineteen out of hundreds, and it took her from June to the middle of September, and she got four of them wrong and had to bring them home again. At the end of it she went up the ladder one last night before school started, expecting — she was not sure what. Some visible dent. Some gap in the rafters where nineteen used to be. The attic looked exactly the same. "It always does," her uncle said, from the crate. "That's not a reason not to." And he left the light on, the way it had always been left on, and they went down and shut the trapdoor, and the humming went on very quietly above them all night, the way it had for years, the way it presumably still does.
